title: Film Workers' Body Asks PM Modi for Foolproof Bollywood Security After Bachchan Shield
excerpt: AICWA's appeal to the Prime Minister follows Amitabh Bachchan's bulletproof-glass Sunday greeting at Jalsa and a string of attacks on film personalities, from Baba Siddique's murder to the firing at Tiger Shroff.
body:
• The All Indian Cine Workers Association (AICWA) has urged Prime Minister Narendra Modi to provide "foolproof security" for Bollywood celebrities.
  • The appeal followed Amitabh Bachchan's Sunday appearance at his Mumbai home Jalsa, where he greeted fans from behind a transparent bulletproof enclosure.
  • AICWA cited the murder of Baba Siddique and attacks on Salman Khan, Saif Ali Khan and Tiger Shroff, asking "who's next?"
  • The workers' body warned that Mumbai must never go back to the underworld days of the 1990s, when the film industry worked under gangland threat.

The sight of Amitabh Bachchan waving to his Sunday crowd from behind bulletproof glass has now reached the Prime Minister's office — at least as a formal appeal. The All Indian Cine Workers Association, the body representing cine workers across the Hindi film industry, has urged Prime Minister Narendra Modi to provide "foolproof security" for Bollywood celebrities, according to a report in The Times of India summarized by Inshorts. The association has also asked for an NIA-level probe and fast-track action, Particle News reported. AICWA's question was blunt: "After the murder of Baba Siddique and attacks on Salman Khan, Saif Ali Khan... and Tiger Shroff, who's next?"

The Sunday ritual that forced the issue

On Sunday, November 1, Bachchan kept his decades-old tradition of greeting fans outside Jalsa, his Juhu bungalow — but from inside a transparent protective enclosure installed on his raised platform, with his son Abhishek Bachchan beside him and security personnel around them, as we reported in our coverage of the appearance. The step-up followed a bomb-threat email about which Mumbai Police received information on October 23. The email named Jalsa and mentioned October 31 and November 27 as dates for alleged attacks, and also named singer-actor Diljit Dosanjh in connection with a purported attack at Mahalaxmi Racecourse on November 27; police have launched an investigation, and the threats were attributed to a group calling itself the "Khalistan National Army," according to IANS reporting. The exact reason for the enclosure has not been officially confirmed.

"After the murder of Baba Siddique and attacks on Salman Khan, Saif Ali Khan... and Tiger Shroff, who's next?"

— All Indian Cine Workers Association

A pattern the industry body wants broken

AICWA's letter is the second time in a fortnight it has gone to the top of government. After shots were fired at Tiger Shroff in Juhu on October 18 — the actor escaped unhurt, but his driver was shot — the association wrote to Home Minister Amit Shah with a list of demands and, in a public statement, set out five asks: the strictest action against the gangsters behind the attacks, the arrest of both the shooters and those who ordered the firing, adequate security for film personalities and their families, accountability for the repeated failure to prevent such attacks, and steps to restore public confidence in law and order, according to Khel Ja's report of the statement. "When a celebrity is not safe in the heart of Mumbai, how can an ordinary Mumbaikar feel safe?" the association asked then. Its president, Suresh Shyamlal Gupta, closed that statement with the line it has now repeated to the Prime Minister: "Mumbai will not be allowed to go back to the underworld days of the 1990s. Bollywood will not work in the shadow of fear."

What happens next

The reports of the letter do not record a public response yet from the Prime Minister's Office, and the Mumbai Police investigation into the threat email naming Jalsa remains the active official thread. For the diaspora audience that grew up on Bachchan's films, the escalation is about an image as much as a policy demand: the Sunday darshan at Jalsa is one of Mumbai's longest-running fan rituals, and it now happens behind glass. Bachchan, meanwhile, continues his screen work, currently hosting the quiz show Kaun Banega Crorepati, even as doctors have advised him to take more rest. Whether the Centre responds with a dedicated security mechanism for film personalities — the task-force idea AICWA raised after the Shroff firing — is now the question the industry is waiting on.
